claims.claim_text: The phantasma proper is what I designate as occupying A_3 in the actualization chain: the determinate presentational image available for cognitive operations.

Phantasia occupies an architectonic position insofar as it orders the transition from aisthēsis to thought (nous), furnishing the phantasmata through which nous and doxa can engage what sensation leaves behind.

claims.claim_text: Heidegger reads Aristotle's account of perception as fundamentally a matter of pathein — being affected by beings as world — wherein the perceiver stands in a relation of being-in-the-world that is already structured by disposition and orientation.

Phantasia names the soul's capacity and activity of generating presentation images from perceptual residue; the phantasma, on the other hand, names the determinate image that results from that activity.

claims.claim_text: Papachristou insists on leaving the Greek word phantasia untranslated precisely because its standard English rendering as 'imagination' obscures the tripartite ambiguity of the term — its simultaneous reference to capacity, activity, and product.

claims.claim_text: Heidegger's phenomenological reading of De Anima III.3-5 understands phantasia as a poiein paron ('making-present') that takes up the eidos or 'look' of what has been perceived and holds it in availability for doxa, memory, and deliberation.
The decisive move in Heidegger's reading is that this making-present is not the activity of a faculty producing inner copies of external objects; it is a mode of being-in-the-world.

What phantasia makes present is the eidos — the look of a being, the 'what it is' — and the hedonic tonality or resonant orexis — the 'how it matters to me'. Phantasia is, therefore, the light in which the look of something is seen and felt.

claims.claim_text: The decisive contrast between cases 1 and 2 is that in case 1 the phantasma-affect (resonant orexis) is layered with drink-pathos simpliciter (because a drink-proper-sensible is firing); in case 2 the phantasma-affect is not layered with drink-pathos simpliciter (because no drink-proper-sensible is firing).

In the nous case (rainwater-in-rock-basin): the eidos 'drink' is held under universal premise (water-as-drink, drink-as-life-sustaining, drink-as-good), and there is no specific phantasma or direct sensory perception of any particular drink-source; nous operates on the phantasma in its most generic, abstract mode.

What we see through all three cases Aristotle identifies is that resonant orexis on the phantasma 'drink' is present everywhere the eidos is held: presently deployed (when seeing the drink-as-realizable-good), retained from memory (memory of the canteen, memory of recent rain), prospectively applied (search for places which could hold rainwater), and even atemporally (nous holds the phantasma abstractly in drink-as-good-universally).

claims.claim_text: The three orientational modes share a common structural character: each is a non-committal cognitive engagement with the phantasma, in the precise sense that none of them, taken on its own, yet makes a truth-claim about what the phantasma presents.

The three modes differ from one another in the intentional direction each brings to the engagement and in the temporal orientation each presupposes: intellection holds the eidos atemporally as universal; memory deploys the phantasma retrospectively as past; the discursive mode projects it prospectively, whether toward future action in the practical case or toward inferred truth in the speculative.

Alongside the three orientational modes, a structurally distinct dimension enters the engagement: doxa, the propositional taking-as-something-true through which the rational animal commits the soul to a truth-claim about what the phantasma has been taken-as.

claims.claim_text: The temporal orientation of intellection is atemporal: the universal, once grasped, is not indexed to past, present, or future; it holds across all the times at which its instances might occur and is not itself situated within the temporal continuum.
However, as Heidegger is right to note, even the nous 'of human beings is not pure' but is grounded, bodily, in phantasia, is determined as bodily being-in-the-world.

Heidegger's gloss adds an implicit temporal dimension: the atemporality of intellection is the atemporality of eidos-grasping. The universal has no date, but its grasp is conditioned on the bodily, temporal availability of the phantasma through which it shows.
claims.interpretive_flag_text: 'Heidegger's gloss adds' — clearly user's interpretive synthesis

claims.claim_text: Atemporality marks the structural boundary between intellection and doxa: to intellect the universal human is to grasp it as conceptual content; to hold a doxa that 'this man is human' is to propositionally ratify a truth-claim in which the universal figures. Nous abstracts; doxa asserts.

Nous can operate without doxa — one can grasp what 'human' is without having yet formed a belief about any particular human — and doxa can operate on the universals that nous supplies. The A_3 actuality produced by intellection is the universal grasped; whether a doxa about that universal also arises is a further question.
The second orientational mode is memory, in which the phantasma is addressed as a likeness of something past.

Memory, as developed in On Memory, presents a distinct cognitive orientation upon the phantasma — one that treats the image not as the bearer of a universal but as a likeness of a past perceptual encounter: 'there is no such thing as memory of the present while present; for the present is object only of perception, and the future, of expectation, but the object of memory is past.'
The object of memory is definitionally, as Frede observes, 'a past experience qua past'. The 'qua past' is essential, and it marks the distinction between memory and phantasia more generally.
Only beings that can perceive time can remember, 'and the organ whereby they perceive time is also that whereby they remember.'

The phantasma in memory functions not merely as a spatial representation of an absent object but as a temporally indexed image that carries within itself the mark of pastness. Not every phantasma is a memory: an image of an apple may arise as a free-floating representation, unassociated with any particular past encounter.
claims.interpretive_flag_recommended: 'functions not merely as X but as Y' is interpretive; add hedging.

claims.claim_text: In addition to the phantasma, memory requires the recognition that the phantasma is the likeness of something one has 'formerly heard or perceived or thought' and is 'neither perception nor conception, but a state or affection of one of these, conditioned by lapse of time'.
The lapse of time is not external to memory as its condition but internal to what memory discloses: the past is marked as past and felt as past within the memorial act itself.

Heidegger's existential analytic casts additional light upon this structure. The ecstatic temporality that he describes as Zeitlichkeit — unfolding in the three ecstases of future, having-been, and present — provides a framework within which the temporal indexing of the memory-phantasma can be understood not as a mechanical timestamp but as a mode of Dasein's self-relation.

claims.claim_text: The third and final orientational mode differs from the other two in a structural respect: it operates not upon a single phantasma but upon several, synthesizing them into a unified object of thought that none of the constituent phantasma alone could furnish.

Aristotle specifies the synthesizing character: 'whether this or that shall be enacted is already a task requiring calculation; and there must be a single standard to measure by, for that is pursued which is greater. It follows that what acts in this way must be able to make a unity out of several images.'

Within this discursive synthetic mode two domains must be distinguished: a practical domain (deliberative or anticipatory phantasia) and a theoretical domain (speculative or theoretical thinking). Both share the underlying synthetic operation upon multiple phantasmata; they differ in the nature of the object they synthesize toward and in whether the synthesis issues in action or terminates in contemplation.

Where sensory phantasia generates phantasmata that are direct residues of past perceptions, deliberative phantasia synthesizes multiple phantasmata into composite images representing states of affairs that have not yet happened and may never happen.

implicit_citations_needed.locus: DA III.10, 433b29 + DA III.11, 434a16-21 (sensory vs calculative phantasia)

claims.claim_text: Two interlocking sub-functions constitute the practical operation: the projective-synthetic sub-function (recombining phantasmata into images of states not yet actual) and the calculative-practical sub-function (measuring projected possibilities against one another by a single standard to determine which course of action shall be enacted).

Deliberative phantasia is essentially prospective or future-oriented; it generates the image of a prospective good or evil that serves as the object of desire and the terminus of practical reasoning. The distinction between sensory and deliberative phantasia is not merely a difference of degree but a difference of cognitive orientation.

Deliberative phantasmata are to some degree under the control of the rational agent, who can summon, combine, and arrange images in the service of practical reasoning. Deliberative phantasia allows rational souls to hold back from what is immediately present by projecting what is future, and this holding-back requires — indeed presupposes — a sense of time.

'While thought bids us hold back because of what is future, desire is influenced by what is just at hand: a pleasant object which is just at hand presents itself as both pleasant and good, without condition in either case, because of want of foresight into what is farther away in time.'

The sense of time is co-implicated with deliberative phantasia: the capacity to calculate and the capacity to perceive time cannot, on Aristotle's account, be separated without destroying both. Deliberation, as Heidegger parses it, is a 'seeking', 'a being-after a definite view that I want to achieve. Through deliberating, I want primarily to come to the telos of a doxa; it is not a yes. I only want to appropriate a definite view regarding a set of facts.'
Speculative thinking constitutes the second dimension of the discursive mode, operating upon the phantasma not in the service of practical deliberation but for the sake of contemplation itself.

Where deliberative phantasia combines phantasmata to construct images of prospective goods or evils, speculative thinking combines and recombines phantasmata to explore intelligible structures like motion and time and the relation between them.

Aristotle marks the distinction quite clearly: 'thought which is concerned with action' differs from 'thought which is speculative and not concerned with action'; the former 'calculates means to an end', while the latter 'moves nothing'.

Practical thought moves because its object is a realizable good that engages orexis; speculative thought does not move because its object is not a realizable good but a truth that is what it is independently of anything the soul might do. However, speculative phantasia is a movement insofar as it is a thinking-through-phantasmata that discovers intelligible relations in the very process of its movement.

claims.claim_text: The temporal orientation of speculative phantasia is atemporal-contemplative: its object neither lies in the past (as with memory) nor in the projected future (as with deliberative phantasia) but stands outside the practical temporal horizon altogether, as what holds and cannot be otherwise.

The A_3 actualities produced by the synthetic mode are twofold. In the practical case, A_3 is the anticipated possibility that has been constructed from a synthesis of phantasmata, evaluated against a single standard of measure, and either adopted or rejected as a course of action to be pursued. In the speculative case, A_3 is the truth contemplated — the universal, essence, or necessary connection grasped through the composed phantasmatic materials — without issuing in any realizable good.

The chain terminates at A_3 for the speculative case: the contemplated truth moves nothing, and no orektikon motion is initiated at M_3 \to M_4 on its basis. Practical deliberation, by contrast, does initiate such motion, for the deliberated possibility discloses, at A_3, a realizable good toward which orexis can be moved.

In each case, the content of A_3 can, for the rational animal, be taken up by a further operation: the orthogonal committal dimension of doxa, which ratifies the content as true and binds the soul to the ratification involuntarily.

claims.claim_text: Aristotle opens his contrast between phantasia and doxa with a claim about the will: 'Imagining lies within our own power whenever we wish (e.g. we can call up a picture, as in the practice of mnemonics by the use of mental images), but in forming opinions we are not free: we cannot escape the alternative of falsehood or truth.'

Phantasia is eph' hēmin — within our power, available to summoning. Doxa is ouk eph' hēmin — not within our power, not available to decision, withheld from the will precisely because it is answerable to something beyond the will.

Heidegger notes the difference between phantasia and doxa: 'Phantasia: the having-present of something without perceiving it directly, the mere presenting-itself. It can be true or false like doxa. It has both possibilities, but it has them, in a certain sense, only from without, while doxa has the possibility in itself. Within the sense of opining itself lies the can — true or false. Dynaton — adynaton (possible — impossible).'
Where the truthood or falsity of phantasia 'is added to it', for doxa 'the being-able-to-be-true-or-false is already contained in the formation of the view'.

claims.claim_text: Where phantasia is a simple making-present, taking-as-something, doxa is the 'yes-saying' that adds logos-dependent ratification. Rationality is precisely what makes the taking-as-something-true-or-false possible and why doxa is only present in rational beings.

One can imagine the coiled object in the shadowed corner of a shed as a snake; one cannot, having definitively seen that it is a rope, then decide to believe it is a snake. The capacity and the inability arise from a single source: doxa is constitutively truth-or-falsehood-bearing, and it is answerable, accordingly, to how things are rather than to how we might wish them to appear.

Doxa is the soul's involuntary taking-as-something-true or taking-as-something-false: when the phantasma is engaged by intellection, memory, deliberation or speculation, doxa pronounces upon the resulting content, committing the soul to the truth or falsity of what is presented.

Thinking issues in propositions — articulations in logos — and doxa is the soul's stance toward those propositions as true or false; it is not a pre-propositional attitude but a response to propositionally structured content.

Where all higher cognition is grounded in the image-based, pre-propositional mode of being-in-the-world that phantasia discloses, doxa names the average everyday discoveredness of 'being-oriented in the world, how human being-there initially has its world there in an average way'.
Doxa, as Heidegger reads Aristotle, is to 'have a view already', 'to be situated thus and so toward the matter', 'a certain yes-saying to that of which I have a view'.
Doxa is a phasis — doxa asserts; it holds a view as already in place — not as a result of inquiry but as the antecedent ground from which inquiry can even begin.

Aristotle specifies the ontological distinctness of doxa with three conditions that phantasia characteristically lacks: 'Opinion involves belief (for without belief in what we opine we cannot have an opinion), and in the brutes though we often find imagination we never find belief. Further, every opinion is accompanied by belief, belief by conviction, and conviction by discourse of reason.'

Belief names the assent that distinguishes doxa from the non-committal entertainment of an image: to opine is to take something as the case, not merely to present it to the mind. Conviction names the binding force of that assent: doxa does not hold its content tentatively but is held by it. Discourse of reason names the medium through which the assent and its binding force operate: doxa is not the bare registration of an appearance but an assertoric articulation of that appearance under the categories that reason makes available.

Doxa and phantasia can deliver contradictory content simultaneously, and this phenomenon demonstrates their ontological distinctness with clarity: 'we imagine the sun to be a foot in diameter though we are convinced that it is larger than the inhabited part of the earth.'

The phantasma is not corrected by the doxa — it persists unchanged, presenting its testimony regardless of what reason concludes — but neither is doxa compelled by the phantasma's apparent testimony. The soul holds two contents at once: the image of the one-foot sun, the belief in the supra-terrestrial sun.

If doxa were identical to phantasia, or if it were merely a modification of the phantasma's content, the simultaneous holding would be impossible: the correction of the image would be the correction of the belief, or the persistence of the image would override the belief.

'Either while the fact has not changed and the observer has neither forgotten nor lost belief in the true opinion which he had, that opinion has disappeared, or if he retains it then his opinion is at once true and false. A true opinion, however, becomes false only when the fact alters without being noticed.'
The phantasma cannot be the bearer of the truth-value; the doxa must be. Doxa is a distinct assertoric act that takes the phantasma as its material yet can override or diverge from its content.

Two distinct operations must be distinguished under the name 'taking-as', and their distinctness is load-bearing for everything that follows. The first is taking-as: the presenting of an object under a determinate form together with its affective valence — phantasia's accomplishment. The second is propositional taking-as-true-or-false: the ratification of the phantasma as a truth-claim about what is the case — doxa's accomplishment.

The phantasma is the settled image that this motion presents to the mind — no more than the formal-epistemic content preserved after the object has withdrawn (the resonant aisthēma) together with the affective valence inherited from perception (the resonant orexis).

claims.claim_text: If phantasia's making-present were itself propositional assertion — if presenting the sun as a foot wide were the same function as committing the soul to the-sun-is-a-foot-wide — then the simultaneous holding of a 'one-foot' phantasma with a 'larger than the inhabited earth' doxa would be impossible.
The persistence of the phantasma shows that phantasia's taking-as is not in the business of asserting truth at all, and therefore is not suppressed when truth is asserted elsewhere.

Doxa arises from this taking-as. When phantasia, through the phantasma, discloses its object as something determinate, the soul does not merely register the image and move on. The soul takes the disclosure as testimony about what is the case, and this taking-as-true-or-false is doxa's originary movement.

O'Gorman captures the external grounding of this operation: 'opinion's external grounding — we form opinions about the world about us, and the world about us forms our opinions...Through phantasia, opinion makes judgments about the world of appearances' that are either true or false.

The ratification is neither a separate cognitive achievement that follows the presentation after some interval nor a deliberate weighing of evidence; it is the soul's involuntary response to the taking-as that phantasia has already accomplished. Phantasia discloses the object as X; the soul, involuntarily, takes X to be the case.

Aristotle marks the asymmetry: 'imagination does not involve opinion based on inference, though opinion involves imagination'. Phantasia can occur without doxa — the brute has images, navigates by them, but does not opine — but doxa cannot occur without phantasia, because the taking-as upon which doxa's propositional ratification operates is supplied by phantasia alone.

Phantasia presents, from A_1 onward, a resonant orexis constitutive of its making-present — the pleasant-or-painful orientation that Aristotle identifies as co-given with perception. This valence suffices, in simple cases, to move the animal: resonant orexis responds to the aspectually presented pleasant or painful object and appetite fires, without any propositional ratification.

claims.claim_text: The structural consequence is that doxa cannot be treated as a fourth cognitive mode parallel to intellection, memory, and discursive phantasia. Each mode orients the soul toward the phantasma's content along a distinct temporal and categorial axis. Doxa, by contrast, does not orient along any such axis; it ratifies along every axis.

One may remember and simultaneously hold a belief about what is remembered; one may deliberate and form opinions about the projected outcomes; one may grasp a universal through intellection and hold a doxa about the truth of the proposition apprehended. Doxa engages upon any orientational mode, adding to each the dimension of involuntary assertoric commitment.

Doxa is not a fourth mode but an orthogonal dimension — the committal layer through which any of the three orientations becomes a truth-claim upon which the soul is bound. To characterize doxa as an orthogonal committal dimension is to insist that it cuts across the three orientation modes, applying its verdict of truth or falsity to any content they produce.

This orthogonality is essential for preserving the autonomy of phantasia from doxa. The phantasma can be generated, manipulated, and combined without any commitment to its truth; doxa enters only when the soul takes a stand upon the content that the phantasma presents.

Doxa is the soul's moment of commitment: the involuntary propositional ratification, grounded in phantasia's taking-as and answerable to how things are, through which appearance becomes truth-claim and generic resonant orexis becomes the determinate mobilization of higher-order emotion.

claims.claim_text: Phantasia supplies the aspectual presentation through the phantasma; doxa binds the soul to the presentation as-true-or-false. What phantasia discloses aspectually, doxa ratifies propositionally; what doxa ratifies, emotion mobilizes into determinate conative form; what emotion mobilizes, action completes.

The propositional taking-as-true-or-false is the hinge of the entire chain for rational animals engaged in evaluatively complex action: the pivot upon which the world's aspectual disclosure becomes the soul's determinate movement.

Burke's observation that Aristotle 'looks upon rhetoric as a means that proves opposites' illuminates the orthogonal character of doxa. The rhetorical capacity to argue for and against the same proposition presupposes that the propositions themselves — grounded in phantasmata — are neutral with respect to truth-value until doxa commits the soul to one side.
Heidegger notes that 'ultimately, rhetoric has its sight on krisis (judgment), view-construction, a definite decision in the sense of a doxa'.

Views are 'cultivated, renewed, established, hardened in speaking' and rhetoric 'is nothing other than the interpretation of being-there with regard to the basic possibility of speaking-with-one-another'.

The orthogonality of doxa is not merely a structural feature of individual psychology but a condition of the possibility of rhetoric itself: only because phantasia operates independently of doxastic commitment can the rhetor construct opposing phantasmata and invite the audience to form a definite view of one doxastic stance over another.

claims.claim_text: The completed cognitive actuality at A_3 is not a single homogeneous state but a multi-dimensional achievement in which several distinct operations converge upon the phantasma stabilized at A_2.

The rational cognitive apparatus engages the phantasma along three orientational axes: the atemporal axis of intellection (universal), the retrospective axis of memory (likeness of past), and the discursive axis of deliberative phantasia (composable into projected future / contemplated unchangeable truths).

These three modes differ from one another in intentional direction and temporal orientation but share a common structural role as non-committal engagements through which the phantasma's content is taken up and processed without yet being ratified as true.

Alongside the three, and structurally distinct from them, operates the committal dimension of doxa, which engages orthogonally upon any orientational mode and adds to each the propositional taking-as-true-or-false through which the soul is bound involuntarily to a truth-claim about what that mode has disclosed.

This four-dimensional architecture is organized, throughout, by the two-level structure of taking-as that governs M_2 \to M_3 as a whole. Phantasia's taking-as is pre-propositional, does not require logos, and is accomplished by phantasia alone. Doxa's propositional taking-as-true is logos-dependent and operates exclusively in rational animals, ratifying what phantasia has presented as a truth-claim about what is the case.
